**2026-11-19.** A patch release. **The SQL audit sink writes in batches,** so on a durable
PostgreSQL the audit journal keeps up with a busy engine instead of falling minutes behind it.
Audit is still best-effort and written behind execution. No configuration key, `q:` namespace,
migration, archive or snapshot format change; a 0.8.0 deployment upgrades by changing the image.

## Before you upgrade

Nothing to check. The audit journal's contents, order and deduplication are unchanged; only the
number of transactions used to write it changes.

## The SQL audit sink writes in batches

With `sutra.audit.sql` on, the audit writer used to give every event its own transaction and
commit, one at a time (about sixteen per process instance). On a durable PostgreSQL that topped
out near 280 events a second, and the journal fell ever further behind a busy engine: on the
relay workload at 50 orders a second it was 85,770 rows (about five minutes) behind when the
last order settled.

The writer now takes whatever queued while its previous write ran, up to 256 events, and writes
it as one multi-row insert per deployment in one transaction. What does not change:

- **Still best-effort, behind execution.** An event is queued and written by the audit writer,
  not inside the transaction of the step that produced it; a crash can still lose the events not
  yet written, exactly as before.
- **Same journal.** Events land in each instance's order, deduplicated per
  `(deployment, instance, seq)`, with dense journal ordinals, so
  `/admin/instances/{id}/history` reads the same.
- **A bad row costs only itself.** A batch that fails is written again event by event.

Measured on the relay workload (two processes per order, 32 audit rows per order, metadata
capture, PostgreSQL with `fsync`, `synchronous_commit` and `full_page_writes` on, 60 s):

| 50 orders/s | 0.8.0 | 0.8.1 | audit off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rows unwritten at the last settle | 85,770 (303 s to catch up) | 0 | — |
| Commits per order | 47.9 | 18.3 | 15.0 |
| WAL flushes per order | 35.2 | 6.3 | 3.0 |
| Engine + database CPU per order | 21.3 ms | 8.8 ms | 5.9 ms |
| Settle p50 / p99 | 19 / 156 ms | 20 / 54 ms | 14 / 26 ms |

What audit still costs is write volume, about 1 KB of WAL per row across its indexes, not
commits.

Library surface: `AuditSink::emit_batch` in `sutra_channels::audit`, with a default that emits
one by one, so an existing sink compiles unchanged and a sink that can write many rows at once
overrides it. `tools/sutra-load-test/relay-bench.sh` takes `AUDIT=<capture>` and reports the
audit backlog.

## Release tooling

`make scan-deps RELEASE=1` and `make scan-image RELEASE=1` (`TRIVY_FRESH_DB=1` for
`scripts/security-scan.sh`) replace Trivy's cached vulnerability database with the latest
published one before scanning; one fetched in the last 15 minutes (`TRIVY_FRESH_DB_MAX_AGE_S`) is
reused. Every scan prints the database's `UpdatedAt`. Without the flag the cached database is
used, as before.

## Image scan

CVE-2026-84786 (libssl3, a DANE-enabled TLS client may dereference a NULL pointer) in the
distroless base has no fixed Debian package. The engine never loads libssl3: on the 0.8.1 binary
`readelf -d` lists libgcc_s, libm, libc and the loader as its only libraries, and the binary holds
no libssl name to load at run time. Nothing in it enables DANE: rustls has none, and the Kafka
client's compiled-in OpenSSL is used only by librdkafka, which never turns DANE on. It is
time-boxed in `.trivyignore.yaml` with the other base-image entries, to 2026-12-16.

## Known

- **`SUTRA.INBOUND.CAPABILITY_MISMATCH` answers HTTP 500.** Unchanged from 0.6.23; a later release
  will answer it with 415.
